title: A king in the centre: open the lines before he hides
outcomes: Finds the line-opening sacrifice against a king that has not castled, with its follow-up
Checks that the king is still in the centre before sacrificing
Declines the same sacrifice once the king has castled
Ignores changes far from the king

steps.text: A king still in the centre is a target when lines can be opened toward him and his pieces cannot cover them in time. To attack him you need **open lines** and attackers that arrive first. The lines usually come from a pawn break (a pawn push that attacks an enemy pawn and opens a line) or a sacrifice. Before you sacrifice, name the lines it opens and the checks or forks that follow. Without a follow-up the sacrifice is a gift.

steps.caption: White to move. Black's king is on e8 and has not castled.

line.say: The bishop takes f7 with check. It leaves c4 and opens the diagonal from b3 toward e6.
In the engine's line the king goes to d7.
Qe6 is checkmate. The bishop on f7 protects the queen.

claims.statement: Bxf7+ is the engine's best move (depth 16).
After Bxf7+ the queen on b3 attacks e6.
The queen on e6 is protected once, by the bishop on f7.

steps.text: This works while his king is still in the centre and you can open lines faster than he can get out. It is a **rule of thumb**, and it fails when he has already castled and developed: the same sacrifice then just loses material. Check the sacrifice and its follow-up every time, and ask what changed since the last position you saw.

steps.title: Same sacrifice, different king
steps.prompt: Predict for each: does Nxg6 work? Then check.

When you see an uncastled king in your own games, which do you check first: whether he can castle, how many pieces you have in play, or which line a sacrifice would open? Say which one you tend to skip.
